items.title: Buttigieg: Democrats Need to Get Serious About Amending the Constitution
items.description: In a conversation at The Atlantic Festival with The Atlantic ’s editor in chief, Jeffrey Goldberg, former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg warned fellow members of the Democratic Party to resist the urge to revert to “the previous status quo” if they regain power in the midterms. It would be a mistake, Buttigieg argued, for Democrats to try to reverse “the damage” of the past two years of the Donald Trump presidency by trying to restore the country to how it looked in 2022 or “whenever we think that America was great.” He said that Democrats instead need to build for the idea that “the next quarter century between here and 2050, which is kind of a make-or-break quarter century for the whole American project, is subject to very different conditions and problems than the ones that we inherited.” Buttigieg—whom many analysts see as a potential 2028 presidential contender—offered examples of what that vision might look like. He called for banning gerrymandering and passing a constitutional amendment to address the deluge of money in politics. “This idea that it is somehow beyond our power to use what is probably the single most elegant feature of the Constitution, which is its capacity to be amended—right?—is a complete failure of ambition and imagination,” Buttigieg said. When asked by Goldberg about the Democratic Socialists of America, Buttigieg responded that he thinks “there’s a temptation to imagine that being bold is the same thing as being kind of maximally ideological.” Sometimes it is the case, Buttigieg said, that the leftmost idea is the boldest. But other, more ideologically moderate projects may require “radical reform to our institutions,” he noted. “I know the commentariat wants to get it all fixed on some left-to-center-to-right spectrum,” Buttigieg continued. “To me, what’s more interesting is: Do we have the right package of base hits and big swings, and are we going after both of them, at the same time, all the time?” The following is an edited transcript of the conversation. Jeffrey Goldberg: I want to get to the state of our civilization, but there’s this thing—and we’ve talked about this already—there’s this thing that’s been bothering me more than most things bothering me in the past few days. The fact that a Vladimir Putin–aligned oligarch, extremely dubious past—as opposed to the oligarchs with a wholesome past— ( Laughter ) Extremely dubious past, funded openly—or not openly, it was discovered, but there’s no secret—funded a two-day celebration for the president of the United States’ son. And we were talking a little bit about how that seems fairly normal in our new reality, but if you actually step back a few years ago, in a Bush presidency, Obama presidency, and told somebody, Oh, yeah, the president of the United States’ kid’s wedding is being underwritten by a Russian oligarch , no one would believe that we’ve entered that level of dystopic reality. So my question is: How screwed are we? Pete Buttigieg: Well, if I thought we were altogether screwed, I wouldn’t be doing this. Goldberg: What would you be doing? Moving to Canada? ( Laughter ) Buttigieg: I guess. Goldberg: I just want to know; he’s got access to different forms of transportation. Buttigieg: Is that what giving up looks like now? Moving to Canada? No, I think it’s symptomatic of this bigger pattern we’ve been in where we stare down something that is completely unacceptable and then just move on. And in some ways, the big thing, the spectacular corruption, actually is harder to face. It’s like if you’re in Washington, D.C., and you walk up to the Washington Monument and you stick your hand on it and you look up—which, by the way, is a fascinating experience if you ever get the chance, because you can walk right up to it—but once you do that, you cannot make out the shape or even the size of the Washington Monument, right? Because it’s right there. And when we have monumental corruption or monumental systemic breakdowns, I think it can have the same effect. Part of what I’m trying to do, as I travel the country, is insist that we’ve got to deal with a whole set of things that we’ve just been talking about being wrong for a long time. I’m not just talking about the near term, the recent shocking, spectacular forms of corruption, like what you mentioned about the wedding or the sentences that are coming out of our mouth, right? Half a billion dollars of crypto money from a foreign prince going to the first family, or the jumbo jet—I mean, we all know this list of things, right? Goldberg: Or renaming a cultural center named after a martyred president for yourself. Buttigieg: For example, and then shutting it down because— Goldberg: Because you ran out of money. Buttigieg: You couldn’t get your way. I mean, even that, right? He becomes chairman of the premier cultural institution in the country, and within two years, it’s shutting down, right? But my point is, there’s something broader, bigger, and longer in the making than even Trump and Trumpism itself. Like, if I said the system is broken, that’ll be the least memorable thing I said all day, right? “The system is broken” is a cliché. Everybody says it. Certainly, every politician says it because it’s true. The weird thing is, we say the system is broken, and then we act as if it wasn’t. We go right back to normal and— Goldberg: The system is broken. What’s for lunch? Buttigieg: Yeah, right? Like, if you’re getting ready for a flight and the captain comes on and mentions in passing that the airplane is broken— ( Laughter ) You’re not going to stay on the plane, right? Goldberg: So that’s one of the things you worked on as secretary of transportation, right? ( Laughter ) Was that a bigger problem than we know about? Because that would be really useful. Buttigieg: No, but that’s the point, right? When lots of planes were crashing in the ’60s and ’70s and ’80s, we did something about it and developed this incredible, civilizational achievement of aviation safety, because we didn’t think it was acceptable to have that happen. And here we are in this political system where everybody knows that the role of money in politics, the unrepresentative nature of Congress, what the Supreme Court has turned into, is a huge problem. And eight years ago, when I was talking about things like Supreme Court reform—pretty lonely position—everybody was looking at me funny. Part of why I was doing that was not only because I believe in Supreme Court reform, but because I believe in elevating our ambition as a country when it comes to reforming things that are obviously broken. And look, at a political level, most of the time, most of what people like me should be talking about is the fact that diesel is at the highest price ever recorded, and the fact that interest rates are higher because of the policies of this administration, and the fact that most of us are paying higher health-insurance premiums because of what the Republicans are doing. But the reality is, those kitchen-table issues have become intractable, because you’ve got this political system kicking the legs out from under the kitchen table. And when people see that day after day after day, then when they see some cases of spectacular corruption by the first family, it’s just all part of that wash of low expectations that we’ve come to have for our politics and our system. Goldberg: Is the system broken, or are people broken? Buttigieg: The system is more broken than people. Goldberg: But when I say people, I mean specific people, like the members of Congress. Buttigieg: Okay, well, some of them. But here’s the thing. Goldberg: I don’t mean our audience. They’re not broken. They look great. Buttigieg: It would be an extraordinary run of bad luck if all of the people that we have elected to Congress over the past few years just randomly turned out to be terrible people, right? That would be just statistically— Goldberg: You say that like that’s science fiction, but I don’t know, I mean, but it doesn’t sound that incredible to me either. Buttigieg: Either something about the system makes people worse, or something about the system is actively selecting worse people, right? It’s not just bad luck, right? And I say this having dealt with the United States Congress quite a bit, and you can see how even people who start out good are incentivized to become less so over time. You sit in a committee hearing, and it’s basically a content farm now. You go in hoping to have some legislative progress, and they look at you and tell you you’re right, and then explain why it’s never going to happen. So we can keep wondering why the people who our system produces and pushes into leadership are deeply flawed, or we can do something to create a system where it’s better than that. Goldberg: I’m focusing on Congress because Congress has abdicated its oversight responsibility to a large degree. The judiciary is—put aside the Supreme Court for a second; you do have federal judges checking executive power. But Congress, in its current form, ain’t. So what do you do? Buttigieg: Get a better Congress. ( Applause ) Goldberg: If you were king. Buttigieg: Let me explain what I mean. Yeah, obviously, in the near term, what I mean is elect better people to Congress, which is why I’ve been to most U.S. states at least once in the past year and a half, trying to campaign for people who I think would make better representatives in Congress than the ones that we’ve got. So there’s that. But what I really mean is: Design a better Congress. For example, one way to make sure that you get better and not worse people in a job is to have a very competitive hiring process. We have 435 seats in the House. Roughly 40 of them are competitive, which means nine out of 10 congressional races are races where you pretty much know who’s going to win before the first vote is even cast. In a 50/50 country, right? Which means it is not an authentic, competitive process. Goldberg: It is the most cost-effective job-protection system ever devised. Buttigieg: Yeah. So we ought to ban gerrymandering nationally. We ought to ban gerrymandering. ( Applause ) And the last reason to have any hesitation about doing that fell when they gutted the Voting Rights Act in the Callais decision, because there was, up until then, an argument that, Look, because these states are badly gerrymandered anyway, the only way we’re getting minority representation is to protect minority districts . Now the Supreme Court has basically established a de facto right to partisan gerrymandering. We can have a law that changes that, right? The role of money in politics, obviously part of the problem here. These are not things that are completely beyond our power to deal with. Goldberg: Well, the Supreme Court has basically said it’s beyond your power, on the role of money in politics. Buttigieg: Right. So we should have a constitutional amendment on that. Goldberg: And is that realistic? Buttigieg: We’ve had 27. ( Laughter ) Goldberg: Not lately, though. Buttigieg: We had a— Goldberg: Stopped doing it. Buttigieg: We had a constitutional amendment so that you couldn’t have a drink. And then, like, 10 years later, we thought that was dumb. And we changed it with another constitutional amendment. So this idea that it is somehow beyond our power to use what is probably the single most elegant feature of the Constitution, which is its capacity to be amended, is a complete failure of ambition and imagination. ( Applause ) There are some other things we can do in the meantime. I was in Montana helping gather signatures for an effort called the Montana Plan, which is using, because of what the Supreme Court has said, instead of setting it up as a regulation on speech—since the Supreme Court has said that, you know, money is speech and corporations are people—you go to the fact that corporations only exist as a function of state law, and corporations actually in state law don’t have rights; they have powers, and those powers are enumerated. And so in the law that makes corporations exist, you just have a feature in there that basically says, You don’t get to be a corporation if you are using your Treasury dollars to manipulate elections . That’s one example of something that is designed to have an effect while we don’t yet have a constitutional amendment. Think of it this way: Citizens United came down, I believe, in 2010. So if the counter to a constitutional-amendment process is That could take 15 years, w ell, if we’d started in 2010, we’d be there, right? This is a level of ambition I think we need to have, or else every time we’re trying to make sure that more people can get health insurance or the minimum wage, which hasn’t been raised, I think, since 2009 or 2007, actually goes up—or any other outcome which a majority of Americans already agree—we’re going to keep getting frustrated. Goldberg: I want to ask you something about an even deeper structure. You know, James Madison had a lot of fears, which is why he designed the system we have. James Madison feared that the rise of the daily newspaper would sink democracy, because the once-a-day addition of new information into the human brain was too much for people. You couldn’t go from emotion to reason before new information came the next day. We’re beyond that now. ( Laughter ) We’re well beyond that. And so the question is—it’s a cognitive question. One of the tricks of the Trump administration is to do so much so quickly that you reach overload. The other part of this is, in the social-media environment in which we have, is it irrational or a sign of poor character for a member of Congress to say, Y ou know what, I’m not going out on a limb, because I’m going to get 10,000 death threats a day on social media, and I exist in that content farm, in another form of that content farm . So what do you do to reintroduce the possibility, the space for reason, logic, contemplation? Buttigieg: I’ve come to realize that we have different levels within us of thinking, of consciousness. And part of the problem with social media is that it speaks to the lizard brain, right? Kind of the least contemplative of our levels of thinking. And there’s no question that the system of rewards and punishments that is kind of dominant in the digital world is not healthy for politics. But that is not the only realm where we can practice politics. So one thing that we can do more of is engage in actual spaces—real, physical spaces where people are actually in a room. And politics is often at its best when the public square is physical. I think about it in terms of how I travel, just when I’m walking around town or going through an airport. And 99.9 percent of people who come up to me are very positive. And that includes some people who say, I don’t agree with you politically, but it’s nice to see you . They’re just kind of excited to see somebody they recognize. Goldberg: Having a human interaction. Buttigieg: Yeah. And it’s not because obviously I have 99 percent support. I know this is a divided country. What that tells me is most people in an actual 3-D interaction aren’t assholes, right? ( Laughter ) Very different from how it is online. So I think one very simple thing is to try to cultivate and create more spaces and environments where those interactions happen. That’s in-person convenings, that’s the public square, that’s third spaces, that’s building social capital around existing physical spaces that bring people together, like schools. It’s also something that is part of why I believe in ideas like national service, creating more opportunities for service. Because when I was in the military, that was definitely an environment where I was side by side with people that I had wildly different political values from, and we quickly learned to trust each other with our lives. And part of that had to do with the extreme pressure of being in a war zone. But part of that just had to do with the fact that this group of people was thrown together and tasked with doing something hard. You know, not everybody needs to be in the military for that to be available to more people. It’s why I think a voluntary but ultimately universal opportunity for service would do a lot of good. It would just rewire our brains in a healthier fashion. Goldberg: The answer to Is Donald Trump a symptom or a cause? is both. Yeah, obviously. The question is what percentage is symptom and what percentage is cause? Is it possible to disaggregate that? Buttigieg: I think of it in terms of the broad symptoms and then the cause of some acute problems. So the symptom stuff—this is what I’m getting at with my systems and reform talk: that if the economic and political and social systems in this country were working, we wouldn’t be here. You don’t get a guy like Trump just out of nowhere, right? So, that’s the evidence. Goldberg: Let’s pause on that. What system in particular, or what aspect of the system would have—I don’t mean the cultural system, rise of reality TV and social media—but what part of the system would have stopped this? Buttigieg: The part I think is worst is the part where in a supposedly representative system of government, people reach consensus, or at least overwhelming majority, that certain things should happen, and then they don’t. That is lethal to people’s confidence in their political system, and it leads, sooner or later, to a pattern where they say, You know what? I’m just going to vote to burn the house down because none of this is working. By the way, just a quick political digression here—it is really interesting that most of those big kind of two-to-one things are actually things that are Democratic positions in Washington. So if I think about, like I mentioned earlier, raising the minimum wage—raising the minimum wage at least to $12 is something a majority of Republicans believe we should do. Background checks on guns: 70, 80, 90 percent. Eighty percent of Republicans, gun owners, think we ought to at least do that. Tax fairness, where the wealthiest people are paying at least as much in their taxes as a percentage as a firefighter—overwhelming majority. And what I’ve realized is we’re actually—Democrats are still getting used to being on the right side of the American public on a lot of issues. Because when I came of age, right—like now, everybody’s pretty much with us on taxes and health care—you know, when I came of age, we were on defense about things like the death tax and welfare reform and all of that. And my first time ever on the ballot was 2010, when Obamacare was the toxic issue that killed the Democrats, right? Now it is the winning issue for Democrats. So some of this is new, and I think Democrats aren’t used to that. But my bigger point is you have all these things where there’s actually two-to-one agreement among the American people on what to do. By the way, even immigration—this is true—the broad framework of a grand bargain on immigration that’s been there the whole time, and then nothing like that happens in Washington. That breeds a kind of cynicism that I think leads you to a guy like Trump. But then back to the cause part. Even a guy like that didn’t have to do things like this. Like, you could imagine some disagreeable populist leader who is presented with the possibility that AI may threaten the continued existence of the human species and does not decide to call that a hoax. It really matters that we happen to have a president who does. Or if you think about what’s happening, if you’re imagining the calculations that are going on in Beijing right now, or Moscow, obviously they are preparing to take advantage of some specific issues that are attached to having a specifically unstable person running the United States of America. And that’s not just some, you know, world historical force. That’s the particular misfortune we have of being led by this particular man at this particular moment. ( Applause ) Goldberg: Right. They’re clapping for instability. ( Laughter ) I want to come back to the global picture in a second, but stay on this interesting subject of the Democrats. There’s been a switch, you’re right. Mainstream Democratic positions are, generally speaking, the more popular positions. How are the Democrats going to mess up in the next two months so that they don’t take Congress back? ( Laughter ) Buttigieg: Look, I feel really good about the tailwind that we have in the next two months. I was just in Tucson, Arizona, where I think JoAnna Mendoza, who’s a Marine drill instructor and a mom, is going to defeat the Republican congressman there. Then we were in southern New Mexico, where we have Gabe Vasquez, extraordinary frontline Democrat. I think he’s going to earn reelection. Just last night, I was up in Tarrytown with Cait Conley, West Pointer, [who] I think is going to defeat Mike Lawler. We have great candidates running great campaigns. What could go wrong? Two things. Well, lots of things could go wrong between now and the election. I’m mostly trying to make sure—obviously I spend all day, pretty much, when I’m campaigning, trying to make sure things go right at the election. What about after the election? Two things I think would be a terrible mistake. One is to revert to the status quo, the previous status quo. I really think that’s going to be a strong temptation to say, Okay, we’re in; we’re going to reverse the damage . You hear the phrase reverse the damage , right? Which is understandable because the damage has been horrific. But the implication of reverse the damage , if that’s going to be our mantra, is, Okay, we’re going to put all these things back just the way they were, and we’re going to give you the world the way it looked in 2022 or 2012 or 1994, or whenever we think America was great . And that’s not going to work. So we’ve got to make sure we resist the temptation to be restoring some previous status quo and build for the new reality that we’re in, with the next quarter century between here in 2050, which is kind of a make-or-break quarter century for the whole American project, is subject to very different conditions and problems than the ones that we inherited. The other thing that I think we need to do is keep it simple in terms of a legislative agenda. So I’ve been thinking a lot about these. For example, one thing that the chattering class will get into right away as soon as there’s hopefully a Democratic victory, is what’s going to be H.R. 1? What’s going to be the big, telltale, Christmas-tree, signature bill that you put all your hopes and dreams in that signifies the priorities of the party and of the new Congress, right? To me, I would like to see, like an H.R. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5—like 10 or 12 dozen things. Stand-alone bills, clean bills, not this ponderous 2,000-page thing that tries to take care of every single thing, but a set of things that are needed, popular, and wise, and will make a difference to people, especially in being able to afford everyday life. So, what does that look like? Restoring the child-tax-credit extension. That puts money back in the pockets of lower-income families trying to raise kids. Obviously, getting us out of a war in Iran that has everybody paying more for gas and diesel. Restoring the help on health care. By the way, also, on the tax side—so usually the revenue part’s unpopular, so you have to tuck that in with the spending part that’s popular. Right now, fixing the tax code so that wealthy tax cheats couldn’t get away with it or even truing up the rates to be a little more normal for wealthy individuals or for corporations—those things are popular on their own. Even if you didn’t staple it to how you’re going to spend the money, just the tax side alone is popular because it’s the right thing to do, and because everybody can tell there’s something wrong with the way things are going. So to me, a rapid fire of clean bills to do these things that everybody—raise the minimum wage, right—these things that everybody knows we ought to do, that’s how we move forward. How do we go wrong? We get tangled up, get in our own way, make it super complicated, and people don’t feel like we’re doing what we actually, hopefully will have gotten elected on, which is making everyday life better, and in particular, making everyday life more affordable. Goldberg: Talk about the DSA temptation. Buttigieg: I mean, look, I think there’s a temptation to imagine that being bold is the same thing as being kind of maximally ideological. To me, sometimes that might be true; sometimes the boldest idea maybe is the leftmost idea. Sometimes I think we’ve reached a point where actually, what I would consider to be kind of ideologically moderate projects—like everything I mentioned, is kind of moderate by definition because two-thirds of Americans want to do it—requires some radical reform to our institutions. And so there are big swings we need to be taking with some of the ones I talked about on reform in the Supreme Court and money and politics and gerrymandering, but also big policy swings, right? I mean, eight years ago, the whole Democratic primary fight in the debates that I was in was about was universal health care going to become mandatory or was universal health care just going to be optional? And not much has changed since then, right? So we also just need to have a higher level of ambition. To me that’s the most interesting thing. I know the commentariat wants to get it all fixed on some left-to-center-to-right spectrum. To me, what’s more interesting is do we have the right package of base hits and big swings, and are we going after both of them at the same time all the time? Goldberg: In the few minutes we have left, talk about the fact that we’re already in World War III and don’t even know it, and while we’re in World War III, the president of the United States is making enemies out of our allies. Buttigieg: Yeah. Goldberg: Discuss. ( Laughter ) Buttigieg: Another essay question. Goldberg: Yeah, you have four minutes—I mean, because this is the Alice in Wonderland cut. We’re trying to have a rational conversation about all the things that you could do to make the lives of Americans somewhat better, you know? And, we have a president right now who seems to want to go to war against Canada, which is a South Park episode. I mean, the question is like, we’re having this conversation, but we’re living in a reality that is South Park . Buttigieg: First of all, every time we see one of these things, we have to remember it doesn’t have to be this way. It doesn’t have to be this way. And politically, what I’m trying to do is connect these things that are happening around the world to issues at home. Because foreign policy always codes as this kind of high-minded, kind of elite concern. But the reality is, foreign policy and what’s going on in the world hits us at home in a million different ways. Like my neighbors in Michigan, you know, a year ago, nobody filling up the pump necessarily had to know or care what was going on in the Strait of Hormuz. It’s not your problem. Now you’ve got gas closer to $5 than $4 in Michigan. Diesel’s through the roof. This is a direct relationship right between what’s going on in the world and what’s going on at home. I was talking with union members in the hospitality industry in Las Vegas, cocktail servers getting fewer hours. Las Vegas has one of the highest unemployment rates in Nevada; generally, in the U.S. Why? Well, one of the reasons is, pissing off Canada meant that Canadians who normally come to southern Nevada, especially in the wintertime, decided to take their money elsewhere, right? So there are these very direct effects on working Americans that happen when you have an absurd foreign policy, like we do. And the result is that it leaves us worse off in the near term economically at home, as well as, of course, the bigger, longer-term picture, which is, we don’t know exactly how and when we’ll need our allies next, but we know that we’ll need our allies. And having alienated them, it’s realistically going to take a generation to have the right level of credibility. Goldberg: This is the question. I mean, let’s assume for a minute that, you know, there’s a Democratic president in the beginning of 2029. How much of what’s happened overseas is reversible and how much is just—I guess the biggest question is, are we, right now, undergoing a midlife crisis, a nervous breakdown, or are we facing a terminal illness? And if you’re sitting in Canada, Paris, London, South Korea, Japan, you’re asking yourself, I don’t know anymore about these people . Buttigieg: Yeah, no, that’s definitely what’s happening. I’ve talked to leaders who—one, who just looked at me and said, “Look, the first time you guys did this, it was,”—this is of a U.S. ally,—“it was a blip. I thought of it as a blip. Now it’s a pattern and our country has to prepare.” And obviously, this scenario where you have a Democratic president next, everybody’s going to be saying, Okay, that’s great, you’re saying all the right things now. But, you know. what’s going to happen in four years? Which is exactly why reversible is not the word on my mind. I’m trying to purge my vocabulary of just about anything with the prefix re in it. But, again, this doesn’t have to be 100 percent negative, because we’re entering into a world where the old patterns and institutions are not coming back. And a lot of those institutions were pretty rickety to begin with. The UN Security Council was set up at a time when the vast majority of people in China were impoverished rural peasants, right? Now, a middle-class city dweller in China arguably has a more technologically sophisticated everyday life than a middle-class city dweller in America. We’re in a very different world in terms of technology, in terms of competition, in terms of the security balance. And so we’re going to need to revamp—there I go, re again. We’re going to need to—I think reimagine is okay. Goldberg: What about refried beans? How do you feel? ( Laughter ) Buttigieg: Ambivalent. Goldberg: Just going out for fried beans from now on. Buttigieg: But I think there’s an opportunity, so it comes back to what I was saying earlier. You know, interpersonally, my experience is you can build trust in a hurry if you are working together on something hard and important. That’s true for people. That’s true for countries. So in addition to the generational project of earning trust and credibility by just consistently doing the right thing and being a dependable friend and ally and a sober voice in the world, there’s also no shortage of very difficult things that we need to be, starting with the response to AI—no shortage of very difficult things where we need to be working with friends, allies, partners, and, in some cases, the whole world. And I think we can quickly earn trust, in the same way that the entire pattern of the U.S. being the most respected and indispensable partner—that was kind of the pattern of the second half of the 20th century—really was built up in a matter of just a few years of doing the right thing when it was really hard. I actually see in that an opportunity, precisely because of how bad it is. I see an opportunity to build something that is going to serve us well for the balance of this century. Goldberg: We’ll find out. Pete, we can do this all day, but we can’t, unfortunately. So, thank you very much for coming.

items.title: U.S. Trade and Development Agency, C-Squared Africa sign deal to expand affordable digital connectivity in Ghana
items.description: The U.S. Trade and Development Agency (USTDA) and C-Squared Africa have signed an agreement for a feasibility study on the deployment of fibre-optic cables along Ghana’s existing electricity infrastructure. The agreement was signed during the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Forum 2026, jointly organised by the American Chamber of Commerce, Ghana (AmCham Ghana), the U.S. Embassy in Accra, the U.S. Commercial Service and USTDA. The forum, held at the Marriott Hotel in Accra on Wednesday, September 9, 2026, brought together government officials, industry leaders and technology partners to discuss Ghana’s AI ambitions under the theme, “AI Deployment and Diffusion: Emerging Opportunities and Supportive Policy.” The feasibility study is expected to support the expansion of affordable and reliable digital connectivity across the country by exploring the use of existing electricity infrastructure for fibre deployment. The signing was witnessed by U.S. Embassy Chargé d’Affaires Rolf Olson and Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovation, Samuel Nartey George. Ghana outlines AI ambitions Speaking at the forum, Mr George outlined the government’s vision for artificial intelligence under the National AI Strategy launched by President John Dramani Mahama on April 24, 2026. He said Ghana’s approach to AI is anchored in national data sovereignty, local capacity building and talent development. The Minister also stressed the importance of partnerships that can transfer technical skills and create sustainable value for Ghanaian businesses. The forum featured discussions on Ghana’s AI infrastructure, market trends, regulation, data protection and public-sector procurement. The infrastructure panel examined the connectivity, power and data-centre requirements needed to support the country’s AI ambitions, with representatives from ATC Ghana, the National Information Technology Agency (NITA), C-Squared and NEDCo. A second panel focused on AI adoption among Ghanaian businesses, including the transition from experimentation to wider enterprise deployment. Participants also highlighted the need for stronger institutional trust and governance, as well as AI solutions developed around Ghanaian data and business realities. Focus on regulation and public-sector adoption Discussions on regulation examined how Ghana’s data protection framework could respond to emerging AI-related issues, including consent, cross-border data transfers and automated decision-making. Representatives from the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovation, the U.S. Department of Commerce and the Telecoms Chamber participated in the session. Another panel examined the procurement of AI technologies for public-sector deployment, with the Ghana Investment Fund for Electronic Communications (GIFEC), World Bank and Ghana Digital Acceleration Project (GDAP) contributing to discussions. Participants considered ways to simplify public-sector technology procurement and discussed calls for a unified digital platform to make business licensing and regulatory compliance easier. The forum concluded with remarks from Enid Kanor, Deputy Chair of AmCham Ghana’s Digital Committee and representative of ATC Ghana, followed by a networking reception.

items.title: La vacunación echa el freno en Europa: “No es que haya colapsado, pero hay señales de alerta”
items.description: Algo está cambiando en Europa respecto a la vacunación infantil, una de las estrategias de salud pública más poderosas y que ha evitado más de 154 millones de muertes en el mundo en medio siglo. Un estudio publicado este jueves en la revista The Lancet Regional Health-Europe sostiene que las coberturas vacunales, que históricamente han seguido una tendencia al alza, se han estancado o han bajado en la mayoría de países de la UE en los últimos años. La situación no es alarmante porque en números absolutos las tasas de pinchazos están por encima del 90% en buena parte del continente, pero este giro en las tendencias es un toque de atención, dicen los autores. Un aviso de que un paso atrás en la vacunación puede hacer emerger graves enfermedades y poner en jaque toda la protección lograda hasta ahora. Seguir leyendo

items.title: N.Korea leader’s sister blasts US drills, threatens ‘more offensive’ response
items.description: The powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un accused the United States of escalating regional tensions through frequent military drills and warned of a “more offensive” response from Pyongyang, according to a statement published by state media Friday. “The present situation, in which new records are set in terms of practical action hostile toward the DPRK, stresses the need to break records in our responsive action, proportional or more offensive in its nature,” the KCNA news agency quoted Kim Yo Jong as saying, using North Korea’s official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. Referring to joint military drills held in recent months by US forces and allies in the Asia-Pacific region as a “US-led war rehearsal,” Kim vowed that “our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence.” “I remind the enemy once again that if it is judged that the supreme interests of our nation and its military sovereignty and security environment in the region have been seriously violated by their military maneuvers,” Kim went on, North Korea’s military will “mobilize all means available to cope with it.” AFP The post N.Korea leader’s sister blasts US drills, threatens ‘more offensive’ response appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: We have at least 6 weeks of fuel cover – NPA boss calms supply fears
items.description: The National Petroleum Authority (NPA) says Ghana currently has at least six weeks of fuel cover, dismissing concerns that the country could face an imminent shortage amid tightening global petroleum supplies. NPA Chief Executive Officer, Godwin Edudzi Tamakloe, said the available stocks, combined with fuel cargoes currently at sea, provide a significant buffer for the domestic market. “Currently, we have not less than 6 weeks of cover. Not less,” he said on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition on Thursday. He was responding to concerns over Ghana’s fuel supply outlook following recent reports of tighter global supplies and reduced fuel exports to some countries in the sub-region. Asked whether the level of stocks was enough, Mr Tamakloe pointed to the number of vessels currently on the high seas carrying petroleum products. “And if you look at the number of vessels even on the high seas, it is significant. So at this point, yes, I have some supply,” he said. The NPA boss said his immediate concern was not the availability of fuel but the potential impact of international market conditions on prices. “No, my major concern now is price,” he said. Asked whether he expected supply problems within the next month, Mr Tamakloe was emphatic. “Not at all,” he said. He explained that developments in the international market were also prompting exporting countries to adjust their strategies, while pointing to the growing role of Nigeria’s Dangote refinery. “Dangote is here,” he said to allay such fears. His comments come as Ghana’s fuel market faces renewed pressure from global supply disruptions linked to conflicts and tighter availability of petroleum products. The International Energy Agency has warned of a significant reduction in global oil supply in 2026, while refined fuel inventories have also come under pressure. The developments have also coincided with fresh increases in Ghana’s fuel price floors. From September 16, the NPA’s floor price rose to GH¢16 per litre for petrol and GH¢16.77 for diesel, with LPG set at GH¢10.97 per kilogramme. Meanwhile, BOSTenergies has clarified that reductions in fuel exports to Burkina Faso and Mali do not indicate an imminent shortage in Ghana. The company said the reduction was largely linked to revamp works at its Bolgatanga depot. Mr Tamakloe also defended Ghana’s private-sector-led downstream petroleum architecture, saying the system was deliberately designed to encourage private-sector participation. He acknowledged concerns that private operators could potentially exert pressure on government but said safeguards had been introduced. “I think there are some buffers that we put in place to ensure that the 2014-2015 events do not happen again. And like I said, that’s a particular concern, a great concern, to the President of the Republic, so we don’t get to a point where the private sector can effectively hold the whole country to ransom,” he said.

items.title: Ouagadougou/Lutte contre les gîtes larvaires : Une opération d’enlèvement de pneus lancée dans l’Arrondissement n°6
items.description: La mairie de l’Arrondissement n°6, en collaboration avec la veille citoyenne, a mené une opération d’enlèvement de pneus abandonnés afin de réduire les gîtes larvaires et protéger la santé des populations. Dans le cadre de la lutte contre les vecteurs de maladies et pour améliorer le cadre de vie des habitants, la mairie de l’Arrondissement n°6, en partenariat avec la veille citoyenne, a organisé une opération d’enlèvement de pneus abandonnés dans plusieurs espaces publics. Ces pneus, laissés à l’air libre, retiennent les eaux de pluie et deviennent des gîtes larvaires favorables à la prolifération des moustiques, vecteurs de maladies comme le paludisme. Cette initiative s’inscrit dans les activités de lutte anti-vectorielle menées par la mairie. Elle vise à assainir l’environnement, réduire les sites de prolifération des moustiques et protéger la santé des populations. Lors de la cérémonie d’ouverture, la mairie a rappelé que la lutte contre les vecteurs de maladies est une responsabilité collective. Elle a invité les habitants à adopter des comportements responsables, notamment en évitant l’abandon de pneus, récipients et autres objets susceptibles de retenir l’eau. La mairie encourage la participation active des populations, des associations et des organisations de veille citoyenne à ces actions d’intérêt collectif. Pour le Chef du projet, il s’agit de développer une véritable culture de prévention et de vigilance face aux risques sanitaires. À travers cette opération, la mairie réaffirme sa volonté de poursuivre les initiatives pour maintenir un environnement sain et salubre dans l’Arrondissement n°6. items.title: Alerte sociale | Expulsion à Pabré : une consultation chez une Adja à Saaba à l’origine de l’accusation
items.description: Accusée d’être à l’origine de la fracture au pied du vieux Rogo, une femme vivant dans un village de Pabré aurait été expulsée de sa communauté en 2025. Une information parvenue à la rédaction de Zoodomail.com. Courant fin de l’année 2025, Joana, une femme dans un petit village de Pabré, aurait été chassée de sa communauté après avoir été accusée de sorcellerie. Selon les informations parvenues à Zoodomail.com, elle aurait été désignée comme responsable de la fracture au pied d’un vieillard du village, dénommé Rogo, dont la blessure aurait du mal à guérir. Dans son récit, cette accusation aurait conduit à son expulsion du village, dans des conditions qu’elle décrit comme particulièrement éprouvantes. Que s’est-il réellement passé ? Une consultation chez une Adja à Saaba à l’origine de l’accusation Selon les informations recueillies par Zoodomail.com, une femme du village, Sonia, se serait rendue à Saaba pour consulter une Adja qui aurait effectué une séance de prière et de révélation. Joana affirme que cette consultation aurait ensuite servi de fondement à son accusation. « Il y avait une Adja à Saaba qui priait pour les gens. Quand elle est allée, elle l’a aspergée d’eau et a fait une révélation, comme quoi la fracture du pied du vieux Rogo était imputable à moi, Joana. Je lui ai demandé et elle a confirmé », selon Joana. La femme explique avoir envisagé de faire appel aux fétiches, avant d’y renoncer sur les conseils de son entourage. Quelques jours plus tard, alors qu’elle se trouvait dans le village, elle aurait découvert un attroupement sous un arbre. Joana raconte qu’en s’approchant de l’attroupement pour comprendre ce qui se passait, elle aurait appris qu’elle était accusée de sorcellerie. « Quand je me suis approchée pour savoir ce qui se passait, c’est là-bas qu’on m’a dit de ramasser mes bagages et de quitter le village dans les minutes qui suivaient parce que je serais une sorcière. » Selon son récit, elle aurait été contrainte de quitter les lieux avec très peu d’effets personnels. « J’ai pu prendre mon petit sac, la CNIB et un peu d’argent. En quittant, ils ont fouillé mon sac pour voir s’il n’y avait pas d’autres âmes que j’emportais avec moi. Ils m’injuriaient et me menaçaient », poursuit-elle. Joana affirme également qu’une fois arrivée dans un village voisin, certaines personnes lui auraient demandé de désigner d’autres personnes qu’elle considérait comme des sorciers. Elle raconte avoir vécu un profond sentiment d’abandon, notamment lorsque son neveu, présent dans la foule, lui aurait déclaré ne plus la reconnaître. Sonia : « Je ne me rappelle pas de ce que l’Adja a dit » Sonia confirme s’être rendue chez une Adja à Saaba, mais dit ne pas se souvenir de la teneur de la révélation. « Oui, je suis allée voir une Adja à Saaba qui m’a aspergée d’eau, mais je ne me rappelle pas de ce qu’elle a dit. » « C’est la fille de Joana qui est rentrée chez nous sans me saluer et, quelques instants après, elle-même est venue me dire que c’est moi qui ai dit qu’elle était sorcière. » Sonia affirme ne pas avoir eu connaissance des propos qui auraient conduit à l’accusation de Joana. « J’ai dit que j’étais allée chez l’Adja, mais je ne me rappelle pas de ce qu’elle a dit. C’est quand je suis revenue du travail dans la soirée que j’ai appris qu’elle avait été expulsée du village pour sorcellerie », affirme-t-elle. Face à cette accusation de sorcellerie, cinq personnes qui auraient participé à l’accusation et à l’expulsion de Joana ont été interpellées par la police, selon les informations recueillies par Zoodomail.com. Alerte sociale Au Burkina Faso, l’accusation de sorcellerie est pénalement réprimée. La loi prévoit des sanctions qui varient notamment selon les conséquences subies par la victime. Selon les dispositions du Code pénal burkinabè relatives à l’accusation de pratique de sorcellerie, les faits peuvent être punis de trois à cinq ans d’emprisonnement lorsqu’ils entraînent notamment l’exclusion sociale de la victime, des coups et blessures ou des dégradations de biens. Les sanctions peuvent être plus lourdes lorsque l’accusation entraîne des conséquences particulièrement graves. Zoodomail.com appelle à la vigilance, à la solidarité et au respect de la personne humaine. Toute personne victime de menaces, de violences ou d’expulsion en raison d’une accusation de sorcellerie peut saisir les autorités compétentes pour faire valoir ses droits. items.title: Why Democrats Might Choose to Impeach Cabinet Members
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. If Democrats win control of the House in November, they will face a dilemma: Should they attempt a record third impeachment of Donald Trump? The president and his allies have warned that this would be a Democratic majority’s first move. “I’m going to be impeached. They’re going to impeach me,” Trump said last month at a rally in South Carolina. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been noncommittal. “We haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out in terms of impeachment,” the would-be speaker told ABC’s This Week on Sunday. But Representative Jamie Raskin, the lead manager of Trump’s second impeachment, seemed more open. Earlier this month, on Meet the Press , he said that Trump had “undoubtedly” committed impeachable offenses. “We understand it’s not a panacea. It is a tool in the toolbox,” he said. “We will not hesitate to use it if we need to use it.” Realistically, House Democrats may have a hard time resisting impeachment. Their voters are in a punchy mood. A new CBS News / YouGov poll found that opposition to Trump is the top motivation for Democratic voters in the midterms, and the political consultant Sarah Longwell recently wrote in The Atlantic that the most important priority for Democratic voters is not left-versus-right ideology but a willingness to fight Trump tooth and nail. Jeffries has already faced criticism for being too passive a leader, as well as for meeting with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and he may struggle to ignore a groundswell of support for impeachment. As a constitutional matter, the case for impeaching the president is solid. Trump has usurped congressional powers, started an unauthorized war or two, defied courts, and used his position for outrageous personal and family enrichment. In 2019, my colleague Yoni Appelbaum made the intellectual case for impeachment as a useful democratic process. The political case for impeaching Trump is shakier. Regardless of the results in November, Democrats are unlikely to get enough votes in the Senate to convict and remove him, meaning that a third impeachment would hit the same dead end as the first two. An impeachment can still be effective as a way of damaging a president, but Trump is already deeply unpopular and will never face voters again, so the upside is limited, and an impeachment might give him a way to rally his remaining base around him—which would only strengthen his power and resolve. But what if House Democrats impeached Trump’s Cabinet members instead? The power to impeach secretaries and other executive-branch officers is explicit in the Constitution but perhaps not well known, because it’s been used only twice in history. One reason such proceedings are rare is that a president usually fires a Cabinet member or forces them to resign before they can be impeached, but Trump has shown serious reluctance to fire aides because of public pressure. The congressional scholar Norm Ornstein has argued that if Trump won’t rein them in, Democrats should. On Tuesday, outgoing Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican, brought new attention to the possibility by moving to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth . GOP leadership promptly shut down all voting until after the election. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached for corruption, but he resigned the same day and the Senate subsequently acquitted him; a number of senators doubted they had jurisdiction post-resignation. (This historical example resurfaced during Trump’s second impeachment trial, which occurred after he’d left office.) In 2024, House Republicans impeached Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas on vague grounds, but the Senate voted to dismiss the charges as unconstitutional without a trial. A Democratic House could plausibly launch impeachment inquiries into several administration officials, many of which would dovetail with investigations that representatives say they already have planned . In some cases, Democratic representatives have already filed articles of impeachment against Cabinet members, including Hegseth, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and Secretary of Education Linda McMahon, but those have gone nowhere in the GOP-led chamber. A new Democratic majority could change that. The conduct of a few particular individuals makes them likely targets for impeachment efforts. Kennedy has done serious damage to American public health, undermining vaccinations and weakening the CDC. At least one Republican senator has accused him of lying about vaccination rules during his confirmation hearings, when he also falsely characterized a trip he took to Samoa. Hegseth has waged an unauthorized war against Iran, for which he seems to have no realistic game plan; mishandled classified information ; possibly violated the Hatch Act by appearing at a fundraiser for a political candidate; and left the armed forces bereft of leadership by firing a slew of qualified generals and admirals. Attorney General Todd Blanche has been instrumental in turning the Justice Department into a partisan tool for persecuting Trump’s political adversaries, and a federal judge rebuked him for his role in Trump’s attempt to set up a $1.8 billion slush fund for political allies. Multiple sources shared with my colleague Sarah Fitzpatrick serious worries about FBI Director Kash Patel’s leadership , including claims of emotional volatility, heavy drinking, and absence from the job. (Patel denied the allegations and sued Fitzpatrick and The Atlantic for defamation, demanding $250 million.) Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, has led a concerted effort to take congressional powers for the White House. As a policy matter, impeachment of some of these officers could be more effective than ordinary investigations would be in halting the egregious actions taken by their offices and departments. It might also have a couple political benefits over impeaching Trump. First, such an effort could escape the Trump vortex: By moving the focus to officials who don’t command the same personal loyalty as Trump, impeachment might allow more emphasis on actual administration actions and policy, instead of on presidential personality. Second, conviction might still be a remote possibility, but GOP senators who are fed up with the White House might be more willing to vote to convict officers than they would be to risk taking on Trump himself. The real question is whether controversial Cabinet secretaries will stick around to see whether Democrats try to target them. A midterm election, especially one that goes poorly for the president’s party, is typically a moment for some secretaries to exit. But Hegseth seems entrenched, continuing to push out rivals ; Blanche just won confirmation; and Kennedy and Vought are ideologues pursuing treasured agendas. If neither they nor Trump are willing to change course, then a Congress that has done little for the past two years will have a chance to do something novel: act. Related: How does impeachment work? ( From 2017 ) How Trump broke—and then saved—impeachment ( From 2021 ) Here are three new stories from The Atlantic : Ian Bogost: College is coming apart. Who made America poorer and dirtier? A plan to pay married mothers not to work Today’s News The White House withdrew President Trump’s nomination of Lance Schroyer to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement after his confirmation stalled in the Senate. Senator Rand Paul, a Republican, had delayed scheduling a confirmation hearing while he sought more information from the Department of Homeland Security about investigations into the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal immigration officers in Minneapolis. Trump was photographed reviewing a poster yesterday that appeared to say Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED , hours before his administration told a federal court that safety concerns required the building to close temporarily. The administration said the closure would last seven days and is separate from the legal dispute over the center’s future. Yesterday, the House passed a bipartisan bill aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher energy costs tied to new data centers . The measure, approved 417–3, would require states to consider standards that make data centers cover the fund of grid upgrades needed to power their facilities. Evening Read Illustration by Olga Aleksandrova The Dead Silence of AI Therapy By Steven Barrie-Anthony Therapy can involve a lot of words, but it’s often the pauses that matter most. If you transcribed a session, the pauses would look like nothing: beats of silence, extra breaths, slowing down. But these can represent the crux of the practice: entry points into feeling. My job as a psychoanalyst is to listen as much to silence as to words, to be present with the patient while they’re quiet—to stay with them as they allow their feelings to emerge. I was trained across diverse theories and techniques, but in my clinical work I have found that the cornerstone of the process is feeling. The patient’s emotional experience is the destination and the terrain. But I also feel; I am moved. And the work I do with my patients relies on our relationship and our capacity for mutual feeling. In many ways, the history of my field from Freud on has been a growing acknowledgement of the reality of this relationship—moving from the therapist as sealed off and standing apart, toward approaches that view the real human relationship between patient and therapist as the territory where healing happens. items.title: Toyin Abraham rejects inclusion in Lagos APC campaign council
items.description: Actress Toyin Abraham has denied her inclusion in the All Progressives Congress Lagos State Campaign Council’s Entertainment and Creative Economy Directorate. The movie star urged the public in an Instagram Story post Thursday to disregard reports suggesting her inclusion in the council. “I’m not a member of any campaign council. I have said it recently. I am staying out of politics. Please disregard the supposed inclusion of my name in any campaign committee,” she wrote. Among the prominent entertainers listed in the directorate are actor Jide Kosoko, actresses Eniola Badmus, Toyin Abraham and Bimbo Akintola, as well as Fuji musicians Wasiu Alabi Pasuma, Abass Akande Obesere and Adewale Ayuba. The campaign council was unveiled on Thursday by the Kadri Obafemi Hamzat Media Centre, ahead of its formal inauguration scheduled for Friday, September 18, 2026, at the APC Secretariat on ACME Road, Ikeja. Toke Benson-Awoyinka is listed as the Director of the Entertainment and Creative Economy Directorate, while Kosoko will serve as Co-Director and Badmus as Deputy Director. Akeem Alimi, popularly known as Ajala Jalingo, was named Secretary, with Dare Olateju serving as Assistant Secretary. Other notable members include veteran actors Adebayo Salami, popularly known as Oga Bello, Saheed Balogun, Bukky Wright, Fathia Balogun, Yinka Quadri and Tayo Sobola. The list also features Abiola Adebayo, Remi Oshodi, Foluke Daramola, Kikelomo Balogun, Bopo Oyekan Ismaila, Rasaq Yusuf, Aderinola Philips, Olamide Maja and Abbey Lanre. Musicians and entertainers on the list include Sulaimon Alao Adekunle, popularly known as Malaika; Akorede Babatunde Okunola, known as Osupa; Temitope Adekunle, popularly known as Small Doctor; Sule Adiro Ataweye; Yemisi Falaye; Leke Babatunde Akinrowo; Kayode Fahm and Aruna Ishola. items.title: Youssou N’Dour à la Primature : la Guinée invitée d’honneur du Grand Bal 2026
items.description: La Guinée sera mise à l’honneur lors de l’édition 2026 du Grand Bal, le rendez-vous culturel porté depuis plusieurs années par l’artiste sénégalais Youssou N’Dour. L’annonce a été faite à l’occasion de sa rencontre avec les autorités guinéennes à Conakry ce jeudi 17 septembre. L’artiste-compositeur sénégalais a été reçu en audience à la Primature par le Premier ministre Amadou Oury Bah, en présence notamment du ministre de la Culture, du Tourisme et de l’Artisanat, Moussa Moïse Sylla, du ministre de la Jeunesse, Lansana Béa Diallo, du ministre des Sports, Cellou Baldé, ainsi que de membres du Cabinet de la Primature. Au cours de cette rencontre, Youssou N’Dour a officiellement remis au chef du Gouvernement les lettres d’invitation destinées à la Guinée pour participer à cette édition du Grand Bal. L’événement, qui figure parmi les rendez-vous culturels majeurs portés par l’artiste sénégalais, entend réunir différentes composantes du continent autour de la culture et du divertissement. Selon Youssou N’Dour, cette initiative s’inscrit dans une démarche visant à contribuer à la promotion d’une image positive de l’Afrique à travers la culture, le sport et la mobilisation des forces vives du continent. Il a également évoqué le programme Simandou 2040, dont l’ambition portée par la Guinée a, selon lui, contribué au choix du pays comme invité d’honneur.

items.title: Fiji declares HIV a national emergency as cases surge
items.description: Fiji has declared a national emergency as HIV cases surge, and is expanding access to testing, treatment and prevention services. About one in 60 adults in the tiny Pacific archipelago is now living with the bloodborne virus, compared with one in 167 five years ago, with a rising number of babies dying from HIV-related complications. The nation of less than a million people saw 2,016 new diagnoses in 2025 alone, Health Minister Antonio Lalabalavu said, noting that “an outbreak-level response is no longer sufficient”. A spiralling trend of drug use, unsafe sex, needle sharing and “bluetoothing” underpins the epidemic, health experts and NGOs earlier told the BBC . “Bluetoothing” or “hotspotting” refers to the dangerous practice where intravenous drug users inject the blood of already intoxicated individuals, which has fuelled a global HIV surge, especially in parts of Africa and in the Pacific. One reason for its appeal is a cheaper high: multiple people can chip in for a single hit and share it among themselves. Another is the convenience of needing only one syringe, which are difficult to come by in Fiji. One in 60 adults live with the bloodborne virus, with a rising number of babies dying from HIV-related complications The Fijian government will introduce a syringe and needle programme as part of its response to the national crisis. The country already has sufficient supplies of syringes and needles, Lalabalavu says, with legislative amendments to be introduced in parliament so that the programme can be rolled out. The minister also urged people to come forward and get tested. “No one should be ashamed, threatened, or excluded because of their HIV status,” he said. “Stigma drives people away from the very services that can help them.” Of the 9,100 Fijians living with HIV in 2025, only 39% knew their HIV status and just 22% were accessing antiretroviral treatment, according to the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV and Aids (UNAIDS). This stands in stark contrast to the global average, where 78% of people with HIV are accessing treatment. Jason Mitchell, who leads the national HIV response taskforce, believes it will take “upwards of five years for [Fiji] to get on top of the epidemic”. “It’s a long-term programme, it’s not something like Covid that’s turned around in two years. HIV is very different,” he told ABC News is an interview. The HIV epidemic has led to a strain on Fiji’s health services, Mitchell said. “For a health system that’s already struggling, to have people who should really be well because there’s treatment available taking up beds in hospitals and sitting in outpatient… Our clinical services has really been under a lot of pressure.” UNAIDS has welcomed Fiji’s emergency declaration, saying it signals the urgency needed to ramp up response to a higher level across government and society. “It is also a stark reminder to the world that Aids is not over. HIV epidemics can change quickly, and countries need health and community systems that are ready to respond urgently,” said the executive director of UNAIDS Winnie Byanyima.

items.title: Hausse illicite des prix des produits à Ouagadougou : 5 boutiques scellées, leurs propriétaires embarqués pour Faso Mêbo
items.description: La Brigade Mobile de Contrôle Économique et de la Répression des Fraudes (BMCRF) a mené une vaste opération dans la capitale et ses environs, sanctionnant les commerçants qui pratiquaient des hausses illégales sur le ciment et les produits de grande consommation. La BMCRF a intensifié ses opérations de contrôle dans la capitale et ses périphéries pour garantir le respect des prix réglementés. Du Grand Marché à Kamboinsin, en passant par les zones de stockage de ciment, les équipes ont inspecté avec rigueur les points de vente. Toute tentative d’augmentation illicite des prix, qu’il s’agisse du ciment ou des produits de première nécessité, a entraîné la fermeture immédiate du commerce concerné et la pose de scellés. Au total, cinq lieux de commerce ont été sanctionnés. Leurs propriétaires ont été interpellés et réquisitionnés pour des travaux d’intérêt général. La BMCRF annonce que ces opérations se poursuivront et seront renforcées. Elle avertit que toute nouvelle infraction conduira à la fermeture du commerce et à des sanctions exemplaires. Par cette répression, la brigade entend protéger les consommateurs et garantir l’application stricte des prix réglementés, afin de préserver le pouvoir d’achat des populations. items.title: Lagos 2027: Egunjobi, Ninolowo dump APC for APM
items.description: By Ebunoluwa Sessou Two politicians who were aspirants on the platform of the All Progressives Congress, APC, for the Lagos State House of Assembly have defected to the Allied Peoples Movement, APM, following changes to the APC’s candidate list for the Agege constituencies I and II. The affected politicians are former Agege Local Government Chairman, Kola Egunjobi, who is seeking the Agege Constituency I seat, and Azeez Yusuf, popularly known as Ninolowo, who is contesting for Agege Constituency II. Vanguard gathered that the two had picked the APM tickets to continue their bids for the Lagos State House of Assembly in the 2027 election. The development followed an earlier dispute over the APC’s selection of candidates for the two constituencies. Egunjobi and Ninolowo had been reported as winners of the APC primaries conducted in May. The results were subsequently followed by changes to the party’s list of candidates, with Oluwagbenga Abiola named for Agege Constituency I and Enimakure Akindele Sakiru named for Constituency II in reports on the revised list. Egunjobi had publicly challenged the outcome in June, alleging that the result of the primary election in Agege Constituency I, did not reflect the votes recorded at the various voting centres. The latest development means that both politicians will now seek to contest the 2027 Lagos Assembly election under the APM platform. Their move has attracted attention in Agege, coming against the backdrop of earlier disagreements within the Lagos APC over the Assembly primary process. The development also coincides with the political transition of the Speaker of the Lagos State House of Assembly, Mudashiru Obasa, who secured the APC ticket to contest the Agege Federal Constituency seat in the House of Representatives in the 2027 election. Obasa emerged as the party’s candidate at the APC primary held in May. The defections add a new dimension to the contest for the two Agege Assembly seats ahead of the 2027 elections, with Egunjobi and Ninolowo now set to pursue their ambitions under the APM. The post Lagos 2027: Egunjobi, Ninolowo dump APC for APM appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for using ants as garnish
items.description: A two Michelin-starred restaurant in Seoul has been fined for using ants as a dessert garnish. The owner of Evett in the South Korean capital was fined 15 million won (£8,144; $10,965), while the company operating the restaurant was fined 10 million won for violating the Food Sanitation Act, local media report. Ants are not among the 10 insect species approved for human consumption in the East Asian nation. The approved list includes grasshoppers, locusts and some silkworms. Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the restaurant’s owner, as well as a 20 million won fine, but the judge took into account the owner’s admission of the charge and lack of prior criminal record. However, the judge is reported to have said that, in addition to violating food standards, heavy metals exceeding standards were detected in the ants when they were tested, meaning the “culpability is not light”. The owner was said to have been unaware that providing ants in food was prohibited in South Korea, as they are used as food elsewhere. Their use as a topping for sorbets at Evett came to light after the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety found online reviews accompanied by photographs. It said the owner had sprinkled three to five ants on certain dishes to give them a “sour taste” over nearly four years, amounting to approximately 49,000 ants used as a garnish. Most of the ants were imported from the US, while some came from Thailand, the ministry said. The owner had argued that they were used in a “small part” of the restaurant’s 15-course menu and that diners were told they could opt for a non-ant alternative topping. Ants are eaten and sometimes even valued as a delicacy in several Asian, African and Latin American cultures. Weaver ants and their eggs are used in Thai and Cambodian cooking, while in Colombia, queen ants are as prized as caviar. The Michelin Guide considers a two-star establishment as one that does “excellent cooking” and is “worth a detour”.
